 IRS Pauses Red-Dyed Diesel Penalties: What Happens Jan. 1?
 Tim Esterdahl 
 Tim Esterdahl
 Tim Esterdahl 
 | November 15, 2026 | 0 comments Tim Esterdahl
 | November 15, 2026
 | 0 comments
 IRS headquarters in Washington, D.C. Photo: G. Edward Johnson / Wikimedia Commons , CC BY 4.0 (resized). 
 The IRS is temporarily waiving federal penalties for using red-dyed diesel on the highway. But there’s a detail that matters if you’re thinking about putting it in your pickup: your state can still enforce its own rules. And the IRS hasn’t said what it will do if there’s still red dye in your tank after Dec. 31.
 When we wrote our original red-dyed diesel explainer , the IRS guidance wasn’t out yet. It is now. Here’s what it covers and what I’d check before filling up.
 What the IRS is actually waiving
 The federal penalty relief covers dyed diesel sold for highway use and used on the highway. File photo: Volvo Trucks. 
 The Oct. 14 IRS announcement covers sales for highway use and use on highways nationwide from Oct. 1 through Dec. 31, 2026. The IRS says it won’t impose the applicable federal penalties and is suspending normal collection and enforcement procedures during that period, including federal on-road dye inspections.
 A separate Oct. 21 announcement covers certain federal paperwork. For covered dyed-diesel tax liability under Section 4041(a), the IRS won’t require a Form 720 filed solely for that liability or require that liability to be reported on an otherwise required return. It won’t require those records to be reconstructed later. Other tax and refund documentation requirements still apply.
 The IRS hasn’t announced blanket forgiveness of the underlying tax. It said it expects to issue additional guidance on postponing payment and will explore whether deferred amounts can be eliminated. I wouldn’t count a federal pump-price savings as guaranteed.
 Why a state line can change the answer
 PUTT’s 2025 Ram 2500 test truck. What’s allowed on the road depends in part on state rules. (Photo: John Cappa) 
 The IRS FAQ specifically says the federal relief does not change state fuel taxes or dyed-fuel rules. Here in Nebraska, for example, the Department of Revenue’s FAQ says qualifying agricultural use is covered under the state’s own order, while other road use remains subject to normal enforcement. That separate Nebraska relief period ends Dec. 23, not Dec. 31.
 So if you’re driving across state lines, look up the fuel-tax rules for each state on the route, not just the one where you bought it. Even if you stay home, a state provision for commercial agricultural use isn’t necessarily permission to fill up for a personal trip.
 What if the fuel in your tank is still red in January?
 Check the fuel requirements in your owner’s manual before changing what you put in the tank. (Photo: John Cappa) 
 The IRS says it is considering a grace period or other measures for residual dye in tanks. As of Nov. 15 we haven’t found a decision. Don’t assume that buying the fuel in December gives you permission to burn it on public roads in January.
 My advice: if you can’t confirm the rules where you’ll be driving, stick with clear highway diesel. And check your manual even if the tax rules cover you. As we explained in our look at diesel truck warranty and fuel requirements , the dye tells you how the fuel was marked for tax purposes. It doesn’t tell you whether it meets the specs your truck calls for.
 We’ll update this section when the IRS issues more guidance on dye left in fuel tanks after Dec. 31.
